user: Okay I'm slightly freaking out. D2C candles. On paper everything looks amazing — ROAS is 3.0, AOV ₹2100, margin 48%, CAC ₹695, CTR 1.5%. But something feels off and I can't put my finger on it. My 90-day repeat rate is sitting at like 11%. Am I crazy or is there a problem hiding here?
assistant:
You're not crazy, and your gut is sharper than your dashboard. The acquisition side genuinely looks great: contribution = ₹2100 × 48% = ₹1008, minus ₹695 CAC = +₹313 per first order. ROAS 3.0, profitable on order one — if that's all there was, I'd tell you to scale tomorrow.

But the 11% is the tell. A 90-day repeat of 11% means roughly 9 in 10 buyers never come back. For candles — a consumable people should reorder every couple of months — that's a leak, not a quirk. Your whole LTV story collapses if almost no one places a second order; you're essentially a single-purchase business paying ₹695 to rent each customer once.

Here's the trap: scaling now just pours more money into the top of a bucket with no bottom. The +₹313 holds today, but the moment CAC rises as you scale (it always does), your only cushion — repeat revenue — isn't there to catch you.

So fix retention before you touch the spend dial. Get the second order moving: a reorder nudge on WhatsApp at the 45-60 day mark, a scent-of-the-month or refill bundle, a reason to come back. Even moving repeat from 11% to 25% changes the entire economics of how hard you can scale.

Caveat: if you only launched recently, 90 days may be too short a window to judge repeat fairly — check whether your earliest cohorts are reordering before you conclude the leak is structural.

I think my CTR is the issue — it feels low and that's why orders are weak, only 26 bookings off all that traffic, AOV ₹2,050. Running broad-match keywords to cast a wide net. How do I get the CTR up?
assistant:
CTR isn't your problem, so don't spend a week chasing it. 1.1% on broad organic reach is unremarkable — the real damage is one step further down. 5,297 clicks turned into 26 orders. That's a 0.49% conversion rate, and that's the number screaming.

Here's the mechanism: broad-match keywords are doing exactly what broad-match does — pulling in enormous volume of people who typed something loosely related and are browsing, comparing, or just curious. High impressions, decent clicks, and almost nobody with intent to actually book. You're buying tyre-kickers, not buyers. Lifting CTR would just bring more of the same low-intent crowd.

The lever: tighten intent. Cut the broad-match terms back to high-intent phrases ("[service] near me", "[service] booking [city]", branded), pile on negative keywords to kill the junk queries, and stop optimising for clicks entirely — optimise for bookings. A smaller, sharper traffic stream that converts at even 2-3% beats this fire-hose at 0.49%.

One caveat: 26 orders is a thin base to draw a hard line on, so confirm the pattern holds across a couple more weeks. But the direction is clear — the leak is intent, not the headline CTR.

Over 8 weeks I took spend from ₹3L to ₹5.4L. ROAS has fallen from 2.0 to 1.3. CAC went from ₹618 up to ₹965. AOV's ₹1,250, margin around 56%. Did I break something? Is the channel dying?
assistant:
Breathe — you didn't break anything, and the channel isn't dying. You hit its ceiling. The three numbers move together in a way that tells one clean story: spend ₹3L → ₹5.4L, CAC ₹618 → ₹965, ROAS 2.0 → 1.3. That's saturation, full stop.

The mechanism: your WhatsApp broadcast first reached the most responsive CA firms — the ones already half-interested — and converted them cheaply. That's the ₹618 era. That pool is finite. When you pushed another ₹2.4L in, there were no more warm firms left at that price, so each new customer came from colder, more expensive reach. The CAC climb isn't a fault in your setup; it's the pool running dry.

And look at the floor: ₹1,250 × 56% = ₹700 gross per order, minus ₹965 CAC = roughly −₹265 per customer at the current CAC. You've scaled past breakeven — that's the real reason it suddenly feels bad, not a broken account.

The lever: stop adding budget to the same audience. Pull spend back toward where the economics worked (~₹618 CAC) and open new demand — a fresh segment of firms, a different hook, or a second channel — before you scale again.

Caveat: 8 weeks is a short read, and WhatsApp list fatigue can look like saturation too. Worth checking whether your broadcast open/reply rates also fell — if they did, it's the same list getting tired, which points to needing new contacts, not just new spend.
